papers.name: Component 1: Performing
papers.covers: Non-examined assessment, marked by the school using Pearson's assessment grids. One solo performance and one ensemble performance, each at least one minute and at least four minutes in total. 30% of the qualification, and nothing the app can revise for.

papers.name: Component 2: Composing
papers.covers: Non-examined assessment. Two compositions, each at least one minute and at least three minutes in total: one to a brief set by Pearson, one free. 30% of the qualification, done in Sibelius and Cubase at this school.

papers.name: Component 3: Appraising
papers.covers: The written exam, and the only component the app covers. 40% of the qualification. Section A is worth 68 marks: six questions on six of the eight set works, a dictation question in which you fill in the missing rhythm and then the missing pitches of a short melody, and one question on an unfamiliar piece. Section B is worth 12 marks: an extended comparison of a set work with an unfamiliar piece from the same area of study, with skeleton scores of both extracts printed in a separate source booklet. Each set-work extract is played three times.

commandWords.meaning: Give the term: usually one mark per term, with no explanation unless the question asks for one.
Give a short factual answer: a key, a tempo marking, an instrument.
Pick out a feature from the extract or the skeleton score.
Say what is happening in the music using correct terms. Two or three marks, so two or three separate points.
Say what is happening and what its effect is, or why the composer did it.

Put both pieces side by side on the same feature, ideally in the same sentence. Short comparison questions in Section A want one difference or similarity per mark. In Section B the examiners' report says direct comparisons must run through the whole answer.
Dictation: write in the missing rhythm, then the missing pitches, on the stave. You hear the tonic chord and the pulse first, and the melody is played four times (2019); five marks for each part.

Section B: judge how effectively each piece uses the elements the question names, for example "Evaluate how effectively ... use instrumentation and music technology". Each evaluative comment must rest on an accurate musical observation, and conclusions are drawn throughout rather than in a separate paragraph.

An effect is named, usually with the elements to cover ("You should refer to dynamics, harmony and rhythm"). Give one precise device for each element; saying how it creates the effect makes the point secure.

assessmentObjectives.meaning: Perform with technical control, expression and interpretation. Carried entirely by Component 1, so it is earned in the practice room rather than revised for.
Compose and develop musical ideas with technical control and coherence. Carried entirely by Component 2, the two coursework compositions.
Demonstrate and apply musical knowledge: the terms, the contexts and the facts about the set works. Assessed across the written exam; in the Section B essay it carries 6 of the 12 marks.

Use appraising skills to make evaluative and critical judgements about music: analysing what you hear and comparing pieces. In the Section B essay it carries the other 6 marks, and it is only credited when it rests on an AO3 observation.

grade9ByQuestionType.looksLike: The exact term, spelled correctly: syncopation, pizzicato, ritardando, plagal cadence. No sentence, no hedging.

grade9ByQuestionType.questionType: Describe the texture or the harmony (2 to 3 marks)
grade9ByQuestionType.looksLike: One precise point per mark, each using a technical term rather than a description in ordinary words. Homophonic with a walking bass, not just the instruments and the tune.
The rhythm sketched on the first hearing and the pitches filled in on later ones, with the given bars used to fix the key and the pulse before writing anything.

grade9ByQuestionType.questionType: Describe how the composer creates an effect (2 to 3 marks)
grade9ByQuestionType.looksLike: One accurate, precise feature for each element the question names, such as dynamics, harmony and pitch: in 2022 "pp", "dissonance" and "large pitch range" scored all three marks. Saying where it happens and what it does costs little, and is the habit Section B rewards.

Organised by the elements the question names, not by piece, with both pieces in every paragraph and no introduction or conclusion. Uses the skeleton scores as evidence with bar numbers, ties each observation to its effect, and draws conclusions as it goes. Marked in four levels (1 to 3, 4 to 6, 7 to 9, 10 to 12); an answer about only one piece cannot go above 6.
Places the piece in its time and purpose, and links the context to something audible: a harpsichord continuo because it is Baroque, a multitracked vocal because it is a 1974 studio recording.
